In addition to efficiency benefits, it is not uncommon to find TOPCon cells priced lower than PERC cells in 2025 (InfoLink Consulting Co. 2025), although our analysis indicates this is due to severe TOPCon cell overcapacity in China. Demand for PERC cells remains in the United States. Because it is an older technology, PERC has more data around outdoor field performance, which can reduce uncertainty around lifetime system performance. Also, at least one U.S. cell producer has said it is faster to get equipment and ramp capacity when choosing PERC over TOPCon (Card 2024), which can be critical when considering incentive expiration dates. In addition, controversy around patents and IP rights for TOPCon limit its adoption. First Solar and Maxeon (a spinoff from SunPower) began to challenge the legality of imports based on TOPCon technology in 2024 (Pickerel 2025d). Only one U.S. cell producer (Talon PV) is known to have licensed the technology from First Solar in 2024. As of the first half of 2025, it is unknown whether the First Solar (Tetrasun) and Maxeon patents are legally all-encompassing enough to disqualify all TOPCon modules, because there are many variations in metallization and layer sequencing, doping, and deposition methods (e.g., low-pressure chemical vapor deposition or plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition). Several Chinese manufacturers being sued by First Solar and Maxeon have also filed lawsuits concerning TOPCon solar, alleging patent infringement. For example, Trina Solar has sued Canadian Solar for $1.5 billion (V. Shaw 2025d), Jinko Solar has sued LONGi (V. Shaw 2025b) and Waaree Energies (V. Shaw 2025c), and JA Solar has sued Astroenergy (Bellini 2024).
